fetched_contents.text: What is the difference between ‘biodegradable’ and ‘compostable’? At present, there is a wide variety of biodegradable and compostable products available on the market. However, the widespread use of these terms can lead to confusion, making it essential to understand their meaning and differences in detail. What is a biodegradable product? A biodegradable product is one that can naturally break down through the action of microorganisms present in the environment, such as bacteria, fungi and algae. It is important to note that biodegradability always depends on the environment in which it is evaluated (soil, water or compost), as environmental conditions directly influence the process. In the case of industrial composting under aerobic conditions (in the presence of oxygen), a material is considered biodegradable when microorganisms transform it into carbon dioxide, water, mineral salts and new biomass. To meet the usual criteria, at least 90% biodegradation must be achieved within a period of 180 days or less, at a controlled temperature of 58 °C ± 2 °C. There are standardised methods used to verify the biodegradability of products, such as ISO, EN and ASTM standards. Examples include: * UNE-EN ISO 14855, for assessing biodegradation in composting conditions. * UNE-EN ISO 17556, for biodegradation in soil, generally at 25 °C and for a maximum duration of up to 2 years. * UNE-EN ISO 14852, which establishes laboratory conditions for biodegradation in aqueous media, at temperatures between 20 °C and 25 °C, with an approximate duration of 6 months (extendable depending on the case). * ASTM D6691, which evaluates the biodegradation of plastic materials in marine environments, at a temperature of 30 °C and for an approximate duration of 10 to 90 days (extendable depending on the case). > In summary, in order to claim that a product is biodegradable, it must pass specific laboratory tests in the corresponding environment, following the standards mentioned above. What is a compostable product? A compostable product is one that can biologically degrade under composting conditions, transforming into carbon dioxide (CO₂), water, inorganic compounds and biomass. This process must produce high-quality compost, without generating toxic residues and without visually distinguishable fragments of the original material. Unlike biodegradability, compostability implies not only the decomposition of the material, but also its safe integration into compost, ensuring that it has no negative effects on the environment or on plant growth. To claim that a product is compostable, it must comply with the requirements established in specific standards. Focusing on the UNE-EN 13432 standard, which defines the general testing scheme applicable to packaging materials, these tests include: * Chemical characterisation of the material, to verify the absence of hazardous substances. * Biodegradation under composting conditions (according to ISO 14855), to evaluate the degree of biological degradation. * Pilot-scale disintegration testing (according to ISO 16929), which analyses the fragmentation of the material during the composting process. * Ecotoxicity tests on higher plants (according to OECD 208), to ensure that the resulting compost does not negatively affect plant development. Together, these requirements guarantee that a compostable material not only degrades, but also contributes to the production of safe, high-quality compost. Difference between biodegradable and compostable plastics Based on the previous definitions, it can be stated that every compostable product is, by definition, biodegradable. This is because compostability requires compliance with a complete set of tests including chemical characterisation, biodegradation under composting conditions, material disintegration and the absence of toxic effects in the resulting compost. However, not every biodegradable product is compostable. A biodegradable material has only demonstrated its ability to decompose in a specific environment and under specific conditions, but it does not necessarily meet the additional requirements that guarantee proper disintegration and the quality of the compost produced. In summary, compostability is a more demanding concept, as it not only involves biodegradation, but also the complete integration of the material into the composting process without generating negative environmental effects. Compostability certifications Products certified as OK Compost INDUSTRIAL are designed to be treated in industrial composting plants. Therefore, they must be disposed of in the organic waste bin, where they are managed under controlled conditions to produce high-quality compost. Meanwhile, the OK Compost HOME certification guarantees that the product can be composted under home composting conditions. Although laboratory tests are similar in both cases, home composting operates at lower temperatures and with longer degradation times. It is important to emphasise that a biodegradable or compostable product is not designed to be abandoned in the environment (cities, countryside, rivers, lakes or the sea). Biodegradation is only guaranteed under specific and controlled conditions, such as composting. Outside this context, neither proper degradation nor environmental impact can be guaranteed. In this field, AIMPLAS has been recognised by certification bodies such as TÜV Austria, DIN Certco and Biodegradable Products Institute to carry out these tests. In addition, these tests are accredited by ENAC, in accordance with compostability schemes based on standards such as UNE-EN 13432, UNE-EN 14995, ISO 18606, ISO 17088 and ASTM D6400. In this way, AIMPLAS provides companies with the necessary tools to certify their products as compostable. fetched_contents.text: EN13432 vs ASTM D6400: Quick FAQ Guide for Export Buyers Quick Summary: EN13432 and ASTM D6400 are equivalent industrial compostability standards—EN13432 applies in Europe, ASTM D6400 in North America. Both require at least 90% biodegradation within 180 days, full disintegration, and eco-safety. EN13432 certifications come from TÜV Austria or DIN CERTCO; ASTM D6400 often comes with BPI certification. For export compliance, brands must carry the appropriate mark and register in EPR systems like LUCID (Germany) or Triman (France), or conform with U.S. regulations to avoid customs delays and greenwashing claims. As global plastic bans tighten and green compliance becomes essential for market access, understanding compostability standards like EN13432 and ASTM D6400 is no longer optional—it’s mission-critical. For export buyers, especially in the food packaging industry, navigating these certifications can determine whether your biodegradable products can legally enter European or North American markets. This guide decodes the differences, legal requirements, and practical steps between EN13432 and ASTM D6400 in an export-ready FAQ format. Whether sourcing compostable packaging or planning global distribution, this article will help you make informed, regulation-compliant decisions. How to Import from China in 2025: Comprehensive Step-by-Step Guide ---------------------------------------- What Is EN13432? EN13432 is the European Union’s harmonized standard defining whether packaging materials are industrially compostable. OK Compost Lable Key criteria: * Minimum 90% biodegradation within 6 months under controlled composting conditions. * Disintegration into fragments <2 mm within 12 weeks. * No toxic residue; must pass heavy metal and ecotoxicity tests. * Requires final product—not just material—testing. Why it matters for exporters: EN13432 certification is legally required for products marketed as “compostable” in the EU under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive 94/62/EC. Without it, products can be rejected at customs or banned from sale. ---------------------------------------- What Is ASTM D6400? ASTM D6400 is the North American standard (especially in the U.S. and Canada) used to evaluate compostable plastics and packaging materials. Core benchmarks: * Biodegradation ≥90% in 180 days in an industrial compost facility. * Physical disintegration within 84 days. * Must not inhibit plant growth or release heavy metals. * Applies to finished items, not raw material alone. Why it’s critical: Many U.S. municipalities require ASTM D6400 compliance before allowing packaging into organic waste streams. It’s also a prerequisite for third-party logos such as the BPI Certification in the U.S. ---------------------------------------- EN13432 vs ASTM D6400: What’s the Difference? Aspect EN13432 (EU) ASTM D6400 (U.S./Canada) Scope Packaging only Broader: packaging + plastics Region European Union North America Biodegradation Timeline 6 months 6 months Testing Per final product Per final product Ecotoxicity Required Required Legal Backing Required by EU law Required by local/state law Labeling EN13432 logo or TÜV Austria BPI logo or ASTM mark 👉 Bottom Line: Both are rigorous compostability standards, but tied to different legal systems. Products aiming for global distribution should ideally comply with both. ---------------------------------------- Do You Need Both Certifications for Export? Yes, if you’re selling into both Europe and North America. For example: * A bagasse takeaway container marketed in Germany must meet EN13432. * The same product shipped to California or New York must meet ASTM D6400 and be BPI-certified to avoid greenwashing claims and legal penalties. Even if your raw material is certified, your final product (e.g., coated paper bowls, PLA cups) must also be certified for the intended market. ---------------------------------------- What Materials Can Be Certified? Material Type Certifiable Under EN13432? Certifiable Under ASTM D6400? PLA (Polylactic Acid) ✅ ✅ Bagasse (sugarcane fiber) ✅ ✅ Coated Paperboard (with compostable lining) ✅ (if tested as whole) ✅ Oxo-degradable Plastic ❌ ❌ Petroleum-Based Plastic ❌ ❌ Only bio-based or compostable polymers and fibers can meet either standard. Oxo-degradable or bio-blended plastics generally do not qualify. ---------------------------------------- Can You Self-Declare Compliance? No. Both standards require third-party certification. * For EN13432: Recognized bodies include TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO (Germany), and AIB Vincotte. * For ASTM D6400: Most reputable in the U.S. is the Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI). Failure to certify through an accredited body can result in: * Customs seizure * Mislabeling fines * Product bans or delisting * Damage to brand trust ---------------------------------------- Is Home Composting Covered? No. EN13432 and ASTM D6400 are for industrial composting. If you want home composting recognition: * In the EU: Get “OK Compost Home” from TÜV Austria. * In Australia: AS5810 is the standard for home compostables. * In U.S.: No nationally accepted home composting standard exists (yet). ---------------------------------------- How Do These Standards Support Plastic Bans? Governments and municipalities are increasingly referencing EN13432 and ASTM D6400 in their legislation to regulate what can be labeled “compostable” or disposed of with organic waste. fetched_contents.text: Navigating Compostability Certifications Impact Take Action Products Company News Unfiltered 1. Home 2. News 3. Navigating Compostability Certifications Sustainability Among the realities of the climate crisis, the term “compostable” has become increasingly prevalent, offering a solution to the mounting problem of plastic pollution, waste reduction and carbon mitigation. However, as consumers and manufacturers alike navigate the complex landscape of certifications for compostable products, questions arise: How can we trust that a product labeled as compostable truly lives up to its claim? What role do third- party certification bodies play in validating these claims? And how can we ensure that compostable products contribute to, rather than detract from, the health of humans and our environment? > We chose to avoid using the BPI logo to head off a monopoly and to call for one standard for compostability certification. Let's delve deeper into the topic by providing a comparison of third-party compostability certifiers and their processes and requirements. This exploration aims to unravel the intricacies of compostability in the industry and offers insights int how we can navigate the complexities of certification and identify products with confidence and clarity. Understanding Certification Bodies At the forefront of compostability certification are several players, each with its own processes. We will highlight the practices of these players in the industry and offer insights into how to navigate the complexities of certification and product identification with confidence, collaboration and clarity. Delve into the specifics: * ASTM International * Known for developing technical standards across various industries, ASTM sets the groundwork for compostability certification with standards like ASTM D6400, D6868, and D8410. While ASTM’s standards are not certifications themselves, they provide foundational protocols for testing compostable materials. * EN STANDARDS * EN Standards, or European Norms, are the European equivalent of ASTM Standards. EN Standards are issued by the European Committee for Standardization (CEN). The goal of such an organization is to create uniformity across producers, consumers, government agencies, and other relevant parties regarding terminology, product specifications, protocols, and more. EN 13432 is established for compostability. * TÜV Austria (OK Compost) * TÜV Austria is internationally recognized and offers both industrial and home compost certifications. Industrial requirements are based largely on the European standard EN 13432. Their certifications require rigorous testing for biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, total fluorine testing, and chemical composition. TUV OK Compost HOME is also widely regarded as the foremost certifier for home compostability ensuring that products are safe and suitable for breaking down in backyard compost systems. * Din certco * Jointly operated by DIN and TÜV Rheinland Group, DIN CERTCO certifies products to ASTM standards as well as the European standard EN 13432. Their certification process includes rigorous testing for biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, total fluorine testing, and chemical composition. * Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI) * A non-profit certifier in North America, BPI uses Din Certco and previously used NSF, as third-party technical reviewers, to verify food contact compostables to ASTM standards. BPI’s certification requires biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, total fluorine testing and chemical composition. As of January 2024, the BPI license agreement required that all certified items and packaging display the BPI logo. * Compost Manufacturing Alliance (CMA) * Established more recently in the US and now Canada, CMA focuses on certifying bioplastics and paper products to ASTM standards. Their process includes the same ASTM laboratory testing and certification requirements as BPI, plus field disintegration testing at industrial composting facilities. * NSF INTERNATIONAL – THIRD-PARTY VERIFIED - ENVIRONMENTAL CLAIMS FOR COMPOSTABILITY * Since 1944, NSF has been a leader in safeguarding public and environmental health through independent standards and processes. As a third-party verifier of environmental claims, NSF conducts thorough desk audits to verify test report reviews, ensuring that products meet stringent compostability criteria. The NSF Verified Environmental Claim mark is more than just a brand logo; it serves as a powerful endorsement of a product’s compostability, promoting trust among consumers and stakeholders. With a foundation built on trust and transparency, NSF ensures that compostability claims are validated with confidence. How Does Each Body Approach Certification? Mini-report on standards and certification systems

The main standards defining biodegradability and compostability are ISO, EN, ASTM, and related international and regional norms. AIMPLAS explains that biodegradability is assessed using standards such as UNE-EN ISO 14855 for composting conditions, UNE-EN ISO 17556 for soil, and UNE-EN ISO 14852 for aqueous media [N2-F1]. For compostability, EN 13432 is the harmonized European standard for packaging materials, and ASTM D6400 is the North American standard for compostable plastics and packaging [N2-R3][N2-R2]. The European Union’s EN 13432 standard is tied to EU law and defines industrial compostability, while ASTM D6400 is used in North America and requires similar criteria for industrial compostability [N2-F2]. Both standards require at least 90% biodegradation within a set timeframe and full disintegration, along with ecotoxicity and chemical safety checks [N2-F1][N2-F2].

Certification requirements differ by standard and market. EN 13432 certification is required for products marketed as compostable in the EU under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive 94/62/EC, and it involves chemical characterisation, biodegradation under composting conditions, pilot-scale disintegration testing, and ecotoxicity tests on higher plants [N2-F1]. ASTM D6400 requires biodegradation ≥90% in 180 days, disintegration, no toxic residue, and compliance with ecotoxicity and heavy-metal requirements [N2-F2]. Both standards require third-party certification and are associated with accredited bodies such as TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO, Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI), and NSF [N2-F1][N2-F4]. BPI certification specifically uses ASTM D6400 as its base standard and may also include ASTM D6868 and D8410 for eligible items, though the latter is limited to cellulosic-fiber-based substrates [N5-F3]. 

Industrial versus home composting certification is separate. EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 apply to industrial composting and do not cover home composting [N2-F2]. In contrast, OK Compost INDUSTRIAL certification is for industrial composting, while OK Compost HOME is for home composting conditions and operates at lower temperatures and longer degradation times [N2-F1]. World Centric notes that TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO, and BPI all use ASTM-style testing, while TÜV Austria also offers home-composting certification [N5-F4]. The practical distinction is that industrial composting is controlled and standardized, whereas home composting lacks the same uniformity and is therefore covered by a separate certification pathway [N2-F1][N5-F3].

Mini-report on processes and science behind biodegradation and composting

Biodegradation and composting are driven by biological and chemical processes. AIMPLAS explains that biodegradable products are broken down by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae in the environment, and the process is environment-dependent [N2-F1]. The European Environment Agency’s materials suggest that biodegradation mechanisms across polymer classes are well studied, and that the degradation of plastics and microplastics involves mechanisms and influencing factors [N3-R2]. Green Dot Bioplastics states that biodegradation is the process by which a plastic product breaks down, and that this depends on the material’s properties and the environment [N3-R4]. Research on microbial degradation of biodegradable plastics also highlights that these plastics are designed for microbial breakdown, with enzymes and pathways playing a central role [N3-R5].

Composting conditions required for certification are specific and controlled. AIMPLAS says that industrial composting under aerobic conditions at around 58 °C ± 2 °C is used to assess biodegradability, with 90% biodegradation required within 180 days [N2-F1]. It also notes that compostability testing in Europe is based on UNE-EN 13432 and includes composting conditions, disintegration testing, and ecotoxicity checks [N2-F1]. BPI’s certification process, which uses ASTM D6400 as its base standard, involves biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, total fluorine testing, and chemical composition testing [N5-F4]. World Centric further explains that ASTM standards provide the foundational protocols for compostability testing, and that EN standards, such as EN 13432, are the European equivalent [N5-F4]. 

Some plastics degrade faster than others because the science behind biodegradation depends on the material’s composition and the environmental conditions. AIMPLAS emphasizes that biodegradation depends on the environment in which it is evaluated, such as soil, water, or compost [N2-F1]. The same source notes that biodegradation in composting conditions uses UNE-EN ISO 14855, while biodegradation in soil is evaluated at 25 °C and for up to 2 years [N2-F1]. That means the same plastic may degrade more quickly in industrial composting than in soil or marine environments because the temperature, moisture, oxygen availability, and microbial community differ. The review on biological degradation of plastics and microplastics also notes that environmental reservoirs and microbial communities influence degradation mechanisms [N3-R2]. Therefore, faster degradation is not just a property of the polymer itself, but also a result of the specific composting conditions and the presence of suitable microorganisms [N3-R2][N3-R4].

Mini-report on practical certification and verification process

The practical certification and verification process for compostable claims depends on standardized testing, third-party assessment, and accredited certification bodies. AIMPLAS states that compostability testing includes chemical characterisation, biodegradation under composting conditions, pilot-scale disintegration testing, and ecotoxicity tests on higher plants [N2-F1]. BPI’s certification process is based on ASTM D6400 and may also use ASTM D6868 and D8410 for eligible items, with ASTM D8410 limited to cellulosic-fiber-based substrates [N5-F3]. World Centric explains that BPI certification requires biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, total fluorine testing, and chemical composition testing [N5-F4]. NSF verification is also used for compostability claims, with a desk audit to verify test reports and ensure compliance [N5-F4]. 

Disintegration and biodegradation requirements are central to verification. AIMPLAS says that compostable products must biodegrade at least 90% within 180 days and disintegrate into fragments <2 mm within 12 weeks [N2-F1]. BPI’s process requires biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical composition checks, while ASTM D6400 requires biodegradation ≥90% in 180 days and disintegration [N5-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also states that disintegration into small pieces within 6 months and biodegradation into CO₂, water, and biomass within 12 months are used in some certification processes [N5-R3]. Ecotoxicity is another key requirement: AIMPLAS notes that compostable products must produce high-quality compost without toxic residues and without negative effects on plant growth [N2-F1]. BPI and World Centric similarly require ecotoxicity and plant-toxicity testing [N5-F4].

Third-party certification and verification work by having independent bodies assess products against the standards and issue a recognized mark or certificate. BPI uses ASTM D6400 as its base standard and relies on third-party technical reviewers to verify food contact compostables [N5-F3]. TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO, and NSF are cited as third-party bodies that perform testing and verification [N2-F1][N5-F4]. World Centric explains that NSF conducts desk audits to verify test reports and that the NSF Verified Environmental Claim mark serves as an endorsement of compostability [N5-F4]. The evidence also emphasizes that both EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 require third-party certification and that self-declaration is not acceptable [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In short, the verification process is science-based, standardized, and independent: products are tested in accredited laboratories, reviewed by third-party technical reviewers, and certified only if they meet all biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical composition requirements [N2-F1][N5-F3][N5-F4].

Mini-report on how bioplastics are categorized

Bioplastics are typically categorized along three main axes: bio-based, biodegradable, and compostable. The European Environment Agency’s materials clarify that biobased plastics are fully or partially made from biological resources rather than fossil raw materials, and that they are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable [N6-R4]. Biodegradable plastics are defined as those that can naturally break down through microorganisms in the environment, while compostable plastics are a subset of biodegradable plastics that degrade under defined conditions and within a specified timeframe without negatively affecting the quality of compost [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The distinction is important: every compostable product is biodegradable by definition, but not every biodegradable product is compostable [N2-F1].

The plastics that fall into each category vary by material type. European Bioplastics lists examples of biodegradable, compostable plastics such as polylactic acid (PLA), polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), and starch-based materials [N1-R4]. The same source also notes that starch-based plastics are among the common bioplastics [N1-R3]. Other bioplastics include cellulose-based, protein-based, and polymer-based materials, though the exact composition can vary [N1-R2]. Bio-based plastics may be fossil-based or partially bio-based; the EU Environment article states that bio-based plastics are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable [N6-R4]. This means a product can be bio-based but still remain conventional in end-of-life behavior.

Biobased and compostable are distinguished from fully biodegradable because biobased refers to the origin of the feedstock rather than the end-of-life behavior, while compostable refers to the performance of the material under specific composting conditions [N4-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4]. Fully biodegradable means the material can break down in the environment, but not necessarily under composting conditions or to a level that produces safe compost. Compostable plastics, by contrast, must meet more rigorous standards including disintegration, biodegradation, ecotoxicity, and chemical safety [N2-F1][N2-F2]. 

Oxo-biodegradable plastics are different because they are not the same as compostable or fully biodegradable plastics. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics [N4-R2]. Oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based, and some sources note that they are usually fossil-based rather than biobased [N4-R4]. This matters because oxo-biodegradables do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics and are not typically classified under EN 13432 or ASTM D6400 [N2-F2][N4-R4]. In short, bioplastics are categorized by origin (bio-based), by degradation behavior (biodegradable), and by end-of-life performance (compostable), with oxo-biodegradable plastics occupying a distinct but often controversial category [N1-R4][N4-R2][N6-R4].

## How bioplastics are categorized in terms of biodegradability and compostability

Bioplastics are categorized along three overlapping but distinct axes: **bio-based**, **biodegradable**, and **compostable**. These categories describe different aspects of a material’s origin and end-of-life behavior, rather than a single universal definition. In other words, a product can be bio-based without being biodegradable or compostable, and a biodegradable product may not necessarily meet the stricter requirements of compostability [N6-R4][N6-R1][N2-F1].

### 1) Categories used to classify bioplastics

The main categories are:

- **Bio-based plastics**  
  Bio-based plastics are made largely or partly from renewable biological resources rather than fossil raw materials. They are not inherently biodegradable or compostable, so bio-based does not guarantee environmental benefit at end of life [N6-R4][N4-R3].

- **Biodegradable plastics**  
  Biodegradable plastics can naturally break down through the action of microorganisms in the environment, but the process depends on the specific environment in which the degradation occurs, such as soil, water, or compost [N2-F1][N3-R4].

- **Compostable plastics**  
  Compostable plastics are a subset of biodegradable plastics. They are defined by the standard conditions and timeframe under which they will biodegrade and produce high-quality compost without harmful residues or negative effects on plant growth [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F1]. Every compostable product is biodegradable by definition, but not every biodegradable product is compostable [N2-F1].

- **Oxo-biodegradable plastics**  
  Oxo-biodegradable plastics are a separate category. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics. They are often fossil-based and do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics [N4-R2][N4-R4].

### 2) Which plastics fall into each category and what they are made from

The branch reports point to a range of common bioplastics:

- **PLA (polylactic acid)**  
  PLA is a well-known biodegradable and compostable polymer. It is made from lactic acid, which is derived from renewable biomass such as corn starch or sugarcane [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **PHA (polyhydroxyalkanoates)**  
  PHA is a family of biodegradable and compostable polymers produced by microorganisms from renewable resources [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **Starch-based plastics**  
  Starch-based bioplastics are another common category. They are made from plant starch and are often used in packaging and disposable products [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **Cellulose-based, protein-based, and other bioplastics**  
  The evidence also mentions cellulose, protein, and other bioplastic types, indicating a broader family of materials beyond PLA and PHA [N1-R2].

- **Fossil-based or partially bio-based materials**  
  Some bioplastics may be only partially bio-based or fossil-based. For example, the evidence notes that bio-based plastics are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable, and that oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based [N6-R4][N4-R4].

### 3) How biobased and compostable are distinguished from fully biodegradable

The key distinction is that:

- **Bio-based** refers to the feedstock origin: the material is made from biological resources rather than fossil fuels [N4-R3][N6-R4].
- **Biodegradable** refers to the end-of-life behavior: the material can break down through microbial action in the environment [N2-F1][N3-R4].
- **Compostable** refers to a stricter end-of-life performance: the material must biodegrade under defined composting conditions, disintegrate, and produce safe compost without toxic residues or negative effects on plant growth [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F1].

So a product can be bio-based but still not biodegradable or compostable, and a biodegradable product may not meet the full requirements of compostability [N6-R4][N2-F1]. Compostable plastics are therefore the most demanding category because they must pass biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical safety tests [N2-F1][N5-F4].

### 4) What oxo-biodegradable plastics are and why they are different

Oxo-biodegradable plastics are different because they are not the same as compostable or fully biodegradable plastics. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based, and some sources say they are usually fossil-based rather than biobased [N4-R4][N4-R2]. This matters because they do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics and are not typically classified under EN 13432 or ASTM D6400 [N2-F2][N4-R4]. In short, oxo-biodegradable plastics occupy a distinct but controversial category that is often misleadingly marketed as “biodegradable” without meeting the full requirements of compostability [N4-R2][N4-R4].

## Standards and certification systems

Biodegradability and compostability are defined by a set of international and regional standards, including **ISO**, **EN**, and **ASTM** standards.

### 5) Which standards define biodegradability and compostability

The evidence identifies several key standards:

- **UNNE-EN ISO 14855**: used to assess biodegradation in composting conditions [N2-F1].
- **UNNE-EN ISO 17556**: used for biodegradation in soil, generally at 25 °C [N2-F1].
- **UNNE-EN ISO 14852**: used for biodegradation in aqueous media [N2-F1].
- **ASTM D6400**: North American standard for compostable plastics and packaging [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **EN 13432**: European harmonized standard for determining whether packaging materials can be classified as industrially compostable [N2-R3][N2-F1].
- **ASTM D6868** and **ASTM D8410**: additional ASTM standards used for certain eligible items, with ASTM D8410 limited to cellulosic-fiber-based substrates [N5-F3].

These standards form the technical basis for certification and verification. EN 13432 is tied to EU law and is the standard used to market compostable products in the EU, while ASTM D6400 is used in North America [N2-F2][N2-F1].

### 6) What each standard requires for certification

Certification requires a package of tests and compliance with environmental and safety criteria:

- **Biodegradation**  
  A minimum of 90% biodegradation is generally required within a defined timeframe, such as 180 days [N2-F1][N2-F2].

- **Disintegration**  
  The material must disintegrate into small fragments within a specified period, often less than 2 mm in size within 12 weeks or 6 months [N2-F1][N5-R3].

- **Ecotoxicity**  
  The compost produced must not inhibit plant growth or generate toxic residues. Ecotoxicity tests on higher plants are required [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Chemical composition and safety**  
  Chemical characterisation is required to verify the absence of hazardous substances, including heavy metals [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Testing on the final product**  
  Both EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 apply to finished items, not just raw material alone [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 7) How certification differs for industrial versus home composting

Industrial composting and home composting are treated as separate certification pathways.

- **Industrial composting**  
  EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 both apply to industrial composting and are the most widely recognized standards [N2-F1][N2-F2]. These standards require controlled, high-temperature conditions and rigorous testing [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Home composting**  
  Home composting is covered by a separate certification system, such as OK Compost HOME in the EU and AS5810 in Australia [N2-F1][N5-F3]. BPI certification can also be used for home composting, though the evidence here is more explicit about industrial certification [N5-F3]. Home composting typically operates at lower temperatures and with longer degradation times than industrial composting [N2-F1][N5-F3].

In other words, industrial composting is the standard against which most certification is measured, while home composting is a narrower and less standardized pathway [N2-F1][N5-F3].

## Processes and science behind biodegradation and composting

Biodegradation and composting are driven by a combination of biological and chemical processes. AIMPLAS explains that biodegradable products are broken down by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae in the environment, and that biodegradation depends on the environment in which it is evaluated [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that biodegradation mechanisms across polymer classes are well studied, and that the degradation of plastics and microplastics involves mechanisms and influencing factors [N3-R2].

### 8) What biological and chemical processes drive biodegradation

The process is microbial, with microorganisms breaking down the polymer into simpler compounds. The review on biological degradation of plastics and microplastics emphasizes that environmental reservoirs and microbial communities influence degradation mechanisms [N3-R2]. Green Dot Bioplastics also states that biodegradation is the process by which a plastic product breaks down, and that this depends on the material’s properties and the environment [N3-R4]. Research on microbial degradation of biodegradable plastics further highlights that these plastics are designed for microbial breakdown, with enzymes and pathways playing a central role [N3-R5].

### 9) What composting conditions are required for certification

Certification requires controlled composting conditions. AIMPLAS states that industrial composting under aerobic conditions at around 58 °C ± 2 °C is used to assess biodegradability, with 90% biodegradation required within 180 days [N2-F1]. World Centric explains that ASTM standards provide the foundational protocols for compostability testing, while EN standards, such as EN 13432, are the European equivalent [N5-F4].

### 10) Why some plastics degrade faster than others

Some plastics degrade faster than others because the science behind biodegradation depends on both the material’s composition and the environmental conditions. AIMPLAS emphasizes that biodegradation depends on the environment in which it is evaluated, such as soil, water, or compost [N2-F1]. It also notes that biodegradation in composting conditions uses UNE-EN ISO 14855, while biodegradation in soil is evaluated at 25 °C and for up to 2 years [N2-F1]. This means the same plastic may degrade more quickly in industrial composting than in soil or marine environments because the temperature, moisture, oxygen availability, and microbial community differ [N2-F1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that faster degradation is not just a property of the polymer itself, but also a result of the specific composting conditions and the presence of suitable microorganisms [N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Practical certification and verification process

The practical certification and verification process is science-based, standardized, and independent. Products are tested in accredited laboratories, reviewed by third-party technical reviewers, and certified only if they meet all biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical composition requirements [N2-F1][N5-F3][N5-F4].

### 11) What tests are used to verify compostable claims

The tests used include:

- **Biodegradation testing**  
  Biodegradation is measured using standardized methods such as ISO 14855, ISO 17556, ISO 14852, and ASTM D6400 [N2-F1][N2-R2].

- **Disintegration testing**  
  Pilot-scale disintegration testing is used to assess fragmentation during composting [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Ecotoxicity testing**  
  Higher-plant ecotoxicity tests are used to ensure the resulting compost does not negatively affect plant growth [N2-F1][N5-F4].

  The material must disintegrate into small fragments within a defined timeframe, often less than 2 mm in size within 12 weeks or 6 months [N2-F1][N5-R3].

- **Biodegradation**  
  At least 90% biodegradation is typically required within 180 days [N2-F1][N2-F2].

- **Ecotoxicity**  
  The compost produced must not inhibit plant growth or generate toxic residues [N2-F1][N5-F4].

Third-party certification and verification work by having independent bodies assess products against the standards and issue a recognized mark or certificate. ## Bottom line

Bioplastics are categorized by **origin** (bio-based), **end-of-life behavior** (biodegradable), and **specific composting performance** (compostable). Oxo-biodegradable plastics are a separate category that often lacks the same environmental benefits as compostable plastics. Mini-report on how bioplastics are categorized

Bioplastics are typically categorized along three main axes: bio-based, biodegradable, and compostable. The European Environment Agency’s materials clarify that biobased plastics are fully or partially made from biological resources rather than fossil raw materials, and that they are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable [N6-R4]. Biodegradable plastics are defined as those that can naturally break down through microorganisms in the environment, while compostable plastics are a subset of biodegradable plastics that degrade under defined conditions and within a specified timeframe without negatively affecting the quality of compost [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The distinction is important: every compostable product is biodegradable by definition, but not every biodegradable product is compostable [N2-F1].

The plastics that fall into each category vary by material type. European Bioplastics lists examples of biodegradable, compostable plastics such as polylactic acid (PLA), polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), and starch-based materials [N1-R4]. The same source also notes that starch-based plastics are among the common bioplastics [N1-R3]. Other bioplastics include cellulose-based, protein-based, and polymer-based materials, though the exact composition can vary [N1-R2]. Bio-based plastics may be fossil-based or partially bio-based; the EU Environment article states that bio-based plastics are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable [N6-R4]. This means a product can be bio-based but still remain conventional in end-of-life behavior.

Biobased and compostable are distinguished from fully biodegradable because biobased refers to the origin of the feedstock rather than the end-of-life behavior, while compostable refers to the performance of the material under specific composting conditions [N4-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4]. Fully biodegradable means the material can break down in the environment, but not necessarily under composting conditions or to a level that produces safe compost. Compostable plastics, by contrast, must meet more rigorous standards including disintegration, biodegradation, ecotoxicity, and chemical safety [N2-F1][N2-F2]. 

Oxo-biodegradable plastics are different because they are not the same as compostable or fully biodegradable plastics. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics [N4-R2]. Oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based, and some sources note that they are usually fossil-based rather than biobased [N4-R4]. This matters because oxo-biodegradables do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics and are not typically classified under EN 13432 or ASTM D6400 [N2-F2][N4-R4]. In short, bioplastics are categorized by origin (bio-based), by degradation behavior (biodegradable), and by end-of-life performance (compostable), with oxo-biodegradable plastics occupying a distinct but often controversial category [N1-R4][N4-R2][N6-R4].

## How bioplastics are categorized in terms of biodegradability and compostability

Bioplastics are categorized along three overlapping but distinct axes: **bio-based**, **biodegradable**, and **compostable**. These categories describe different aspects of a material’s origin and end-of-life behavior, rather than a single universal definition. In other words, a product can be bio-based without being biodegradable or compostable, and a biodegradable product may not necessarily meet the stricter requirements of compostability [N6-R4][N6-R1][N2-F1].

### 1) Categories used to classify bioplastics

The main categories are:

- **Bio-based plastics**  
  Bio-based plastics are made largely or partly from renewable biological resources rather than fossil raw materials. They are not inherently biodegradable or compostable, so bio-based does not guarantee environmental benefit at end of life [N6-R4][N4-R3].

- **Biodegradable plastics**  
  Biodegradable plastics can naturally break down through the action of microorganisms in the environment, but the process depends on the specific environment in which the degradation occurs, such as soil, water, or compost [N2-F1][N3-R4].

- **Compostable plastics**  
  Compostable plastics are a subset of biodegradable plastics. They are defined by the standard conditions and timeframe under which they will biodegrade and produce high-quality compost without harmful residues or negative effects on plant growth [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F1]. Every compostable product is biodegradable by definition, but not every biodegradable product is compostable [N2-F1].

- **Oxo-biodegradable plastics**  
  Oxo-biodegradable plastics are a separate category. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics. They are often fossil-based and do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics [N4-R2][N4-R4].

### 2) Which plastics fall into each category and what they are made from

The branch reports point to a range of common bioplastics:

- **PLA (polylactic acid)**  
  PLA is a well-known biodegradable and compostable polymer. It is made from lactic acid, which is derived from renewable biomass such as corn starch or sugarcane [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **PHA (polyhydroxyalkanoates)**  
  PHA is a family of biodegradable and compostable polymers produced by microorganisms from renewable resources [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **Starch-based plastics**  
  Starch-based bioplastics are another common category. They are made from plant starch and are often used in packaging and disposable products [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **Cellulose-based, protein-based, and other bioplastics**  
  The evidence also mentions cellulose, protein, and other bioplastic types, indicating a broader family of materials beyond PLA and PHA [N1-R2].

- **Fossil-based or partially bio-based materials**  
  Some bioplastics may be only partially bio-based or fossil-based. For example, the evidence notes that bio-based plastics are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable, and that oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based [N6-R4][N4-R4].

### 3) How biobased and compostable are distinguished from fully biodegradable

The key distinction is that:

- **Bio-based** refers to the feedstock origin: the material is made from biological resources rather than fossil fuels [N4-R3][N6-R4].
- **Biodegradable** refers to the end-of-life behavior: the material can break down through microbial action in the environment [N2-F1][N3-R4].
- **Compostable** refers to a stricter end-of-life performance: the material must biodegrade under defined composting conditions, disintegrate, and produce safe compost without toxic residues or negative effects on plant growth [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F1].

So a product can be bio-based but still not biodegradable or compostable, and a biodegradable product may not meet the full requirements of compostability [N6-R4][N2-F1]. Compostable plastics are therefore the most demanding category because they must pass biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical safety tests [N2-F1][N5-F4].

### 4) What oxo-biodegradable plastics are and why they are different

Oxo-biodegradable plastics are different because they are not the same as compostable or fully biodegradable plastics. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based, and some sources say they are usually fossil-based rather than biobased [N4-R4][N4-R2]. This matters because they do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics and are not typically classified under EN 13432 or ASTM D6400 [N2-F2][N4-R4]. In short, oxo-biodegradable plastics occupy a distinct but controversial category that is often misleadingly marketed as “biodegradable” without meeting the full requirements of compostability [N4-R2][N4-R4].

## Standards and certification systems

Biodegradability and compostability are defined by a set of international and regional standards, including **ISO**, **EN**, and **ASTM** standards.

### 5) Which standards define biodegradability and compostability

The evidence identifies several key standards:

- **UNNE-EN ISO 14855**: used to assess biodegradation in composting conditions [N2-F1].
- **UNNE-EN ISO 17556**: used for biodegradation in soil, generally at 25 °C [N2-F1].
- **UNNE-EN ISO 14852**: used for biodegradation in aqueous media [N2-F1].
- **ASTM D6400**: North American standard for compostable plastics and packaging [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **EN 13432**: European harmonized standard for determining whether packaging materials can be classified as industrially compostable [N2-R3][N2-F1].
- **ASTM D6868** and **ASTM D8410**: additional ASTM standards used for certain eligible items, with ASTM D8410 limited to cellulosic-fiber-based substrates [N5-F3].

These standards form the technical basis for certification and verification. EN 13432 is tied to EU law and is the standard used to market compostable products in the EU, while ASTM D6400 is used in North America [N2-F2][N2-F1].

### 6) What each standard requires for certification

Certification requires a package of tests and compliance with environmental and safety criteria:

- **Biodegradation**  
  A minimum of 90% biodegradation is generally required within a defined timeframe, such as 180 days [N2-F1][N2-F2].

- **Disintegration**  
  The material must disintegrate into small fragments within a specified period, often less than 2 mm in size within 12 weeks or 6 months [N2-F1][N5-R3].

- **Ecotoxicity**  
  The compost produced must not inhibit plant growth or generate toxic residues. Ecotoxicity tests on higher plants are required [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Chemical composition and safety**  
  Chemical characterisation is required to verify the absence of hazardous substances, including heavy metals [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Testing on the final product**  
  Both EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 apply to finished items, not just raw material alone [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 7) How certification differs for industrial versus home composting

Industrial composting and home composting are treated as separate certification pathways.

- **Industrial composting**  
  EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 both apply to industrial composting and are the most widely recognized standards [N2-F1][N2-F2]. These standards require controlled, high-temperature conditions and rigorous testing [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Home composting**  
  Home composting is covered by a separate certification system, such as OK Compost HOME in the EU and AS5810 in Australia [N2-F1][N5-F3]. BPI certification can also be used for home composting, though the evidence here is more explicit about industrial certification [N5-F3]. Home composting typically operates at lower temperatures and with longer degradation times than industrial composting [N2-F1][N5-F3].

In other words, industrial composting is the standard against which most certification is measured, while home composting is a narrower and less standardized pathway [N2-F1][N5-F3].

## Processes and science behind biodegradation and composting

Biodegradation and composting are driven by a combination of biological and chemical processes. AIMPLAS explains that biodegradable products are broken down by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae in the environment, and that biodegradation depends on the environment in which it is evaluated [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that biodegradation mechanisms across polymer classes are well studied, and that the degradation of plastics and microplastics involves mechanisms and influencing factors [N3-R2].

### 8) What biological and chemical processes drive biodegradation

The process is microbial, with microorganisms breaking down the polymer into simpler compounds. The review on biological degradation of plastics and microplastics emphasizes that environmental reservoirs and microbial communities influence degradation mechanisms [N3-R2]. Green Dot Bioplastics also states that biodegradation is the process by which a plastic product breaks down, and that this depends on the material’s properties and the environment [N3-R4]. Research on microbial degradation of biodegradable plastics further highlights that these plastics are designed for microbial breakdown, with enzymes and pathways playing a central role [N3-R5].

### 9) What composting conditions are required for certification

Certification requires controlled composting conditions. AIMPLAS states that industrial composting under aerobic conditions at around 58 °C ± 2 °C is used to assess biodegradability, with 90% biodegradation required within 180 days [N2-F1]. It also notes that compostability testing in Europe is based on UNE-EN 13432 and includes composting conditions, disintegration testing, and ecotoxicity checks [N2-F1]. BPI certification uses ASTM D6400 as its base standard, with biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, total fluorine testing, and chemical composition testing required [N5-F4]. World Centric explains that ASTM standards provide the foundational protocols for compostability testing, while EN standards, such as EN 13432, are the European equivalent [N5-F4].

### 10) Why some plastics degrade faster than others

Some plastics degrade faster than others because the science behind biodegradation depends on both the material’s composition and the environmental conditions. AIMPLAS emphasizes that biodegradation depends on the environment in which it is evaluated, such as soil, water, or compost [N2-F1]. It also notes that biodegradation in composting conditions uses UNE-EN ISO 14855, while biodegradation in soil is evaluated at 25 °C and for up to 2 years [N2-F1]. This means the same plastic may degrade more quickly in industrial composting than in soil or marine environments because the temperature, moisture, oxygen availability, and microbial community differ [N2-F1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that faster degradation is not just a property of the polymer itself, but also a result of the specific composting conditions and the presence of suitable microorganisms [N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Practical certification and verification process

The practical certification and verification process is science-based, standardized, and independent. Products are tested in accredited laboratories, reviewed by third-party technical reviewers, and certified only if they meet all biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical composition requirements [N2-F1][N5-F3][N5-F4].

### 11) What tests are used to verify compostable claims

The tests used include:

- **Biodegradation testing**  
  Biodegradation is measured using standardized methods such as ISO 14855, ISO 17556, ISO 14852, and ASTM D6400 [N2-F1][N2-R2].

- **Disintegration testing**  
  Pilot-scale disintegration testing is used to assess fragmentation during composting [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Ecotoxicity testing**  
  Higher-plant ecotoxicity tests are used to ensure the resulting compost does not negatively affect plant growth [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Chemical composition and heavy-metal testing**  
  Chemical characterisation is required to verify the absence of hazardous substances and heavy metals [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Total fluorine testing**  
  Total fluorine testing is also part of the verification process [N5-F4].

### 12) What disintegration, biodegradation, and ecotoxicity requirements are

- **Disintegration**  
  The material must disintegrate into small fragments within a defined timeframe, often less than 2 mm in size within 12 weeks or 6 months [N2-F1][N5-R3].

- **Biodegradation**  
  At least 90% biodegradation is typically required within 180 days [N2-F1][N2-F2].

- **Ecotoxicity**  
  The compost produced must not inhibit plant growth or generate toxic residues [N2-F1][N5-F4].

### 13) How third-party certification and verification work

Third-party certification and verification work by having independent bodies assess products against the standards and issue a recognized mark or certificate. BPI uses ASTM D6400 as its base standard and relies on third-party technical reviewers to verify food contact compostables [N5-F3]. TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO, and NSF are cited as third-party bodies that perform testing and verification [N2-F1][N5-F4]. World Centric explains that NSF conducts desk audits to verify test reports and that the NSF Verified Environmental Claim mark serves as an endorsement of compostability [N5-F4]. The evidence also emphasizes that both EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 require third-party certification and that self-declaration is not acceptable [N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Bottom line

Bioplastics are categorized by **origin** (bio-based), **end-of-life behavior** (biodegradable), and **specific composting performance** (compostable). Oxo-biodegradable plastics are a separate category that often lacks the same environmental benefits as compostable plastics. The standards that define these categories include **ISO**, **EN**, and **ASTM** standards, with **EN 13432** and **ASTM D6400** being the most common industrial compostability standards. Certification requires biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical safety testing, and it is performed by third-party bodies. Industrial composting is the standard pathway, while home composting is a narrower and less standardized pathway [N2-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3][N5-F4].

The main standards defining biodegradability and compostability are ISO, EN, ASTM, and related international and regional norms. AIMPLAS explains that biodegradability is assessed using standards such as UNE-EN ISO 14855 for composting conditions, UNE-EN ISO 17556 for soil, and UNE-EN ISO 14852 for aqueous media [N2-F1]. For compostability, EN 13432 is the harmonized European standard for packaging materials, and ASTM D6400 is the North American standard for compostable plastics and packaging [N2-R3][N2-R2]. The European Union’s EN 13432 standard is tied to EU law and defines industrial compostability, while ASTM D6400 is used in North America and requires similar criteria for industrial compostability [N2-F2]. Both standards require at least 90% biodegradation within a set timeframe and full disintegration, along with ecotoxicity and chemical safety checks [N2-F1][N2-F2].

Certification requirements differ by standard and market. EN 13432 certification is required for products marketed as compostable in the EU under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive 94/62/EC, and it involves chemical characterisation, biodegradation under composting conditions, pilot-scale disintegration testing, and ecotoxicity tests on higher plants [N2-F1]. ASTM D6400 requires biodegradation ≥90% in 180 days, disintegration, no toxic residue, and compliance with ecotoxicity and heavy-metal requirements [N2-F2]. Both standards require third-party certification and are associated with accredited bodies such as TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO, Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI), and NSF [N2-F1][N2-F4]. Industrial versus home composting certification is separate. EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 apply to industrial composting and do not cover home composting [N2-F2]. World Centric notes that TÜV Austria, DIN CERTCO, and BPI all use ASTM-style testing, while TÜV Austria also offers home-composting certification [N5-F4]. ## How bioplastics are categorized in terms of biodegradability and compostability

Bioplastics are categorized along three overlapping but distinct axes: **bio-based**, **biodegradable**, and **compostable**. These categories describe different aspects of a material’s origin and end-of-life behavior, rather than a single universal definition. In other words, a product can be bio-based without being biodegradable or compostable, and a biodegradable product may not necessarily meet the stricter requirements of compostability [N6-R4][N6-R1][N2-F1].

### 1) Categories used to classify bioplastics

The main categories are:

- **Bio-based plastics**  
  Bio-based plastics are made largely or partly from renewable biological resources rather than fossil raw materials. They are not inherently biodegradable or compostable, so bio-based does not guarantee environmental benefit at end of life [N6-R4][N4-R3].

- **Biodegradable plastics**  
  Biodegradable plastics can naturally break down through the action of microorganisms in the environment, but the process depends on the specific environment in which the degradation occurs, such as soil, water, or compost [N2-F1][N3-R4].

- **Compostable plastics**  
  Compostable plastics are a subset of biodegradable plastics. They are defined by the standard conditions and timeframe under which they will biodegrade and produce high-quality compost without harmful residues or negative effects on plant growth [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F1]. Every compostable product is biodegradable by definition, but not every biodegradable product is compostable [N2-F1].

- **Oxo-biodegradable plastics**  
  Oxo-biodegradable plastics are a separate category. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics. They are often fossil-based and do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics [N4-R2][N4-R4].

### 2) Which plastics fall into each category and what they are made from

The branch reports point to a range of common bioplastics:

- **PLA (polylactic acid)**  
  PLA is a well-known biodegradable and compostable polymer. It is made from lactic acid, which is derived from renewable biomass such as corn starch or sugarcane [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **PHA (polyhydroxyalkanoates)**  
  PHA is a family of biodegradable and compostable polymers produced by microorganisms from renewable resources [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **Starch-based plastics**  
  Starch-based bioplastics are another common category. They are made from plant starch and are often used in packaging and disposable products [N1-R4][N1-R3].

- **Cellulose-based, protein-based, and other bioplastics**  
  The evidence also mentions cellulose, protein, and other bioplastic types, indicating a broader family of materials beyond PLA and PHA [N1-R2].

- **Fossil-based or partially bio-based materials**  
  Some bioplastics may be only partially bio-based or fossil-based. For example, the evidence notes that bio-based plastics are not necessarily biodegradable or compostable, and that oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based [N6-R4][N4-R4].

### 3) How biobased and compostable are distinguished from fully biodegradable

The key distinction is that:

- **Bio-based** refers to the feedstock origin: the material is made from biological resources rather than fossil fuels [N4-R3][N6-R4].
- **Biodegradable** refers to the end-of-life behavior: the material can break down through microbial action in the environment [N2-F1][N3-R4].
- **Compostable** refers to a stricter end-of-life performance: the material must biodegrade under defined composting conditions, disintegrate, and produce safe compost without toxic residues or negative effects on plant growth [N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F1].

So a product can be bio-based but still not biodegradable or compostable, and a biodegradable product may not meet the full requirements of compostability [N6-R4][N2-F1]. Compostable plastics are therefore the most demanding category because they must pass biodegradation, disintegration, ecotoxicity, and chemical safety tests [N2-F1][N5-F4].

### 4) What oxo-biodegradable plastics are and why they are different

Oxo-biodegradable plastics are different because they are not the same as compostable or fully biodegradable plastics. They are designed to fragment in the presence of oxygen, but they do not fully biodegrade in the same way as compostable plastics [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that oxo-biodegradable plastics are often fossil-based, and some sources say they are usually fossil-based rather than biobased [N4-R4][N4-R2]. This matters because they do not meet the same certification standards as compostable plastics and are not typically classified under EN 13432 or ASTM D6400 [N2-F2][N4-R4]. In short, oxo-biodegradable plastics occupy a distinct but controversial category that is often misleadingly marketed as “biodegradable” without meeting the full requirements of compostability [N4-R2][N4-R4].

## Standards and certification systems

Biodegradability and compostability are defined by a set of international and regional standards, including **ISO**, **EN**, and **ASTM** standards.

### 5) Which standards define biodegradability and compostability

The evidence identifies several key standards:

- **UNNE-EN ISO 14855**: used to assess biodegradation in composting conditions [N2-F1].
- **UNNE-EN ISO 17556**: used for biodegradation in soil, generally at 25 °C [N2-F1].
- **UNNE-EN ISO 14852**: used for biodegradation in aqueous media [N2-F1].
- **ASTM D6400**: North American standard for compostable plastics and packaging [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **EN 13432**: European harmonized standard for determining whether packaging materials can be classified as industrially compostable [N2-R3][N2-F1].
- **ASTM D6868** and **ASTM D8410**: additional ASTM standards used for certain eligible items, with ASTM D8410 limited to cellulosic-fiber-based substrates [N5-F3].

These standards form the technical basis for certification and verification. EN 13432 is tied to EU law and is the standard used to market compostable products in the EU, while ASTM D6400 is used in North America [N2-F2][N2-F1].

### 6) What each standard requires for certification

Certification requires a package of tests and compliance with environmental and safety criteria:

- **Biodegradation**  
  A minimum of 90% biodegradation is generally required within a defined timeframe, such as 180 days [N2-F1][N2-F2].

- **Disintegration**  
  The material must disintegrate into small fragments within a specified period, often less than 2 mm in size within 12 weeks or 6 months [N2-F1][N5-R3].

- **Ecotoxicity**  
  The compost produced must not inhibit plant growth or generate toxic residues. Ecotoxicity tests on higher plants are required [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Chemical composition and safety**  
  Chemical characterisation is required to verify the absence of hazardous substances, including heavy metals [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Testing on the final product**  
  Both EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 apply to finished items, not just raw material alone [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 7) How certification differs for industrial versus home composting

Industrial composting and home composting are treated as separate certification pathways.

- **Industrial composting**  
  EN 13432 and ASTM D6400 both apply to industrial composting and are the most widely recognized standards [N2-F1][N2-F2]. These standards require controlled, high-temperature conditions and rigorous testing [N2-F1][N5-F4].

- **Home composting**  
  Home composting is covered by a separate certification system, such as OK Compost HOME in the EU and AS5810 in Australia [N2-F1][N5-F3]. BPI certification can also be used for home composting, though the evidence here is more explicit about industrial certification [N5-F3]. Home composting typically operates at lower temperatures and with longer degradation times than industrial composting [N2-F1][N5-F3].

In other words, industrial composting is the standard against which most certification is measured, while home composting is a narrower and less standardized pathway [N2-F1][N5-F3].

## Processes and science behind biodegradation and composting

Biodegradation and composting are driven by a combination of biological and chemical processes. AIMPLAS explains that biodegradable products are broken down by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae in the environment, and that biodegradation depends on the environment in which it is evaluated [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that biodegradation mechanisms across polymer classes are well studied, and that the degradation of plastics and microplastics involves mechanisms and influencing factors [N3-R2].

### 8) What biological and chemical processes drive biodegradation

The process is microbial, with microorganisms breaking down the polymer into simpler compounds. The review on biological degradation of plastics and microplastics emphasizes that environmental reservoirs and microbial communities influence degradation mechanisms [N3-R2]. Green Dot Bioplastics also states that biodegradation is the process by which a plastic product breaks down, and that this depends on the material’s properties and the environment [N3-R4]. Research on microbial degradation of biodegradable plastics further highlights that these plastics are designed for microbial breakdown, with enzymes and pathways playing a central role [N3-R5].

### 9) What composting conditions are required for certification
